catalog_quote: Roots which contain a vowel usually have that vowel longer than other vowels in the word. The next to the last syllable in the word (regardless of the length) is characterized by the 'word accent' - a noticeable rise in pitch. In most simple words in Kituba the root vowel is also the vowel of the next to the last syllable and thus length and pitch rise coincide. However, many Kituba words have derivational extensions added to the root to make extended stems. In such words the long syllable and the accented syllable do not coincide ... The interplay of the long vowels of roots with the pitch accent of the next to last syllable in the word accounts for the characteristic rhythm of Kituba. ... [Introduction:] In addition to the segmental phonemes listed above, Kituba employs stress and pitch differences. sweep_summary: One Glottolog title item (Ngalasso 1991, Études créoles 14(2):147-162, Persée DOI 10.3406/ecreo.1991.1369) — full per-page text was already on file from the 2026-09-16 fetch and was read end to end. It describes the eastern (Bandundu, DRC) variety — strictly kitu1246 territory, though Glottolog files it under kitu1245 and the catalog's own deciding source (FSI 1963) is also a DRC-side proxy. Ngalasso CONTRADICTS the catalog's framing: the dynamic word accent (energy + length) is root-initial 'quel que soit le schème tonal', 'pas automatiquement sur la pénultième'; the penultimate pitch rise is lexical tone scheme I (H on first root syllable, the majority Kongo-heritage pattern) alongside five other productive tone schemes (final-H French loans, all-low Lingala loans, prefix-H Bandundu loans, all-H themes), so 'l'idée d'une montée de la voix régulière sur la pénultième est une impression superficielle'. Reconciliation: FSI already places root-vowel length on the root and the pitch rise on the penult; Ngalasso and FSI agree on both prominences and disagree on which is the 'accent' and on tone-language status. Mufwene 2009 (author-site PDF, catalog tree) keeps the penult accent(= H tone) framing with an 'important proportion' of all-low/final-H exceptions. Additional open text fetched sources this sweep: Peace Corps Zaire Kikongo trainer manual (ERIC ED294442) — silent on stress. none on archive.org): Fehderau 1966 Cornell thesis (marginal tone contrast, quoted second-hand; medium), Lumwamu 1983 Munukutuba lexical note (the only kitu1245-proper item, holds the penult-accent position per Ngalasso; medium), Mfoutou 2009 Grammaire et lexique munukutuba (variety-matched grammar, unknown content; high). Recommendation: keep 'fixed' but flag the record as contested on WHICH prominence is stress (root-initial dynamic vs penult pitch) and as tone-coexisting; do not treat Ngalasso as superseding FSI for kitu1245 because of the variety mismatch. written at

new_statements.quote: « l'énergie articulatoire caractéristique de l'accent dynamique du kikongo se localise en un point très précis à l'intérieur de l'unité lexicale : généralement sa place se trouve sur la première syllabe de la racine, quel que soit par ailleurs le schème tonal. Cette règle semble toujours en vigueur en kikongo véhiculaire. L'accent est particulièrement perceptible dans les formes prononcées avec une grande insistance : la voyelle accentuée a tendance à être prononcée plus longue que les autres. Les exemples qui suivent montrent clairement 1° que l'accent ne se confond pas systématiquement avec un ton haut; 2° que sa place n'est pas automatiquement sur la pénultième. » (p.159) — « un accent à fonction strictement contrastive dont la place, toujours en début de la racine ou de la base lexicale, est, dans ce sens, totalement prédictible » (p.160)
new_statements.translation: The articulatory energy characteristic of the dynamic accent of Kikongo is located at a very precise point inside the lexical unit: as a rule its place is on the first syllable of the root, whatever the tone pattern. This rule seems still in force in vehicular Kikongo. The accent is especially perceptible in forms pronounced with great emphasis: the accented vowel tends to be pronounced longer than the others. The examples that follow show clearly (1) that the accent is not systematically identical with a high tone; (2) that its place is not automatically on the penultimate. — an accent with a strictly contrastive function whose place, always at the beginning of the root or lexical base, is in that sense fully predictable.
new_statements.citation: Ngalasso, Mwatha Musanji. 1991. Tons ou accents ? Analyse des schèmes tonals du kikongo parlé dans la région de Bandundu (Zaïre). Études créoles 14(2): 147-162. DOI 10.3406/ecreo.1991.1369
new_statements.reading: First-hand description (author is a native-area linguist) of eastern Kikongo-Kituba (Bandundu, DRC): word accent = dynamic (intensity + length) prominence fixed on the ROOT-INITIAL syllable, morphologically anchored and weight-blind; the penultimate high pitch that Swift & Zola 1963 and Mufwene call the 'word accent' is analysed as lexical tone (scheme I, H on first root syllable, the majority Kongo-heritage pattern) coexisting with five other tone schemes (final-H French loans, all-low Lingala loans, prefix-H Bandundu loans, all-H themes, VI). If the catalog's category is 'stress', this puts it at root-initial (= penult only in CV-root+FV words, antepenult or earlier in extended stems), i.e. it contradicts 'penult regardless of length'; it is however consistent with FSI's own observation that root vowels are long while the pitch rise is penultimate — the two sources locate the two prominences identically and disagree only on which one is 'the accent'.

sources.citation: Ngalasso, Mwatha Musanji. 1991. Tons ou accents ? Analyse des schèmes tonals du kikongo parlé dans la région de Bandundu (Zaïre). Études créoles 14(2): 147-162. DOI 10.3406/ecreo.1991.1369 (Persée; PDF altcha-protected, full text recovered from per-page HTML views).
sources.quote: Reports that Lumwamu 1983 (Munukutuba) and Welmers 1973 analyse vehicular Kikongo as an accent language with a predictable pitch rise on the penult, and concedes that northern (Brazzaville) and western (Boma-Matadi) broadcast speech gives a strongly accentual, Swahili-like impression; argues that in the EASTERN Bandundu variety six lexical tonal schemes survive (I (B)(B)HB canonical/majority, II final-H French/Lingala loans, III all-L Lingala loans, IV-VI) alongside a root-initial length accent, so 'penult accent' there is 'une impression superficielle'.
sources.locator: p.147 (position of Welmers 1973/Lumwamu 1983: vehicular Kikongo lost tone, 'montée de la voix... presqu'invariablement sur la pénultième'; Brazzaville/northern dialect broadcasts sound strongly accentual); pp.157-159 (six tonal schemes in eastern/Bandundu Kituba; scheme I (B)(B)HB canonical and 'le plus proche d'une structure accentuée sur la pénultième'; dynamic accent = length on first root syllable); pp.160-161 conclusion (tone not lost 'du moins en ce qui concerne la variété orientale parlée en région de Bandundu').

sources.citation: Mufwene, Salikoko S. 2009. Kituba, Kileta, or Kikongo? What's in a name? In C. de Féral (ed.), Le nom des langues III (BCILL 124), 211-222. Louvain: Peeters.
sources.quote: « Kituba has a predominantly fixed accent system, with the accent borne by the penultimate syllable, quite typically in any of its names. To be sure, as observed by Mufwene (1989a) and Ngalasso (1989), Kituba has an important proportion of polysyllabic words either with only low tones (e.g., mùntù LL 'person', mùnòkò LLL 'mouth, opening' …) ; or with a high tone on the last syllable or on both the penultimate and last syllables (e.g., nzìlá LH 'way, road' … màbélé LHH 'breasts, milk'). However, the majority of the words have only one accent (high tone) borne by the penultimate syllable (e.g., dísù HL 'eye', kwísà HL … kàpítà LHL 'foreman') … Derivative words and conjugated verbs are especially subject to this tone placement rule »
sources.note: Covers Kituba of RC, DRC and Angola. Predominantly fixed penultimate accent (= high tone), stable under derivation/conjugation (kù+pés+à ~ kù+pès+íl+à), with 'an important proportion' of all-low or final-H polysyllables; no grammatical tone. Mufwene cites Ngalasso's 1989 conference version of the 1991 paper for the exception classes but keeps the penult-accent framing.
